title: What if you had the eyes of a mantis shrimp?
sources: National Geographic, 'The mantis shrimp sees like a satellite' (Ed Yong, 2014): https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/the-mantis-shrimp-sees-like-a-satellite
Mapping Ignorance, 'Mantis shrimps (part 2): lords of colour (or perhaps not)': https://mappingignorance.org/2014/03/24/mantis-shrimps-part-2-lords-colour-perhaps/

shots.text: You wake up with the eyes of a mantis shrimp. They have 12 types of color receptors. You had 3.
shots.say: You wake up with the eyes of a mantis shrimp. They have twelve types of colour receptors. You had three.

shots.text: By the end of today, you'll lose a color test to a regular human.
But first, the upgrades. Four of your new receptors see ultraviolet.
shots.say: But first, the upgrades. Four of your new receptors see ultra-violet.

shots.text: You can even see a spiralling kind of light that, as far as we know, no other animal can.
Four times the receptors. So colors must look four times better, right?
Scientists actually tested this on real mantis shrimp. Two lights. Pick the right color, get a snack.
A normal human can tell two colors apart when they're just 5 nanometres different.
shots.say: A normal human can tell two colours apart when they're just five nanometres different.

shots.text: Mantis shrimp eyes? They need 15 to 25.
shots.say: Mantis shrimp eyes? They need fifteen to twenty-five.

shots.text: More receptors, but worse at telling colors apart. Why?
Your human brain compares three signals to blend millions of shades. That takes work, but it's precise.
Scientists think shrimp eyes skip the comparing. Each receptor just shouts its own color. Fast, but blunt.
Perfect for a shrimp that has to spot dinner and punch it, fast.
Useless for you. You got twelve color receptors, and you still can't pick the right paint.
Which animal's sense would you steal instead? Tell me below.
